Where Next

We are actively identifying airports where additional sensor deployment would most benefit open performance monitoring. Priority criteria include:

  • Airports with limited or no existing ADS-B ground station coverage in the OpenSky Network
  • Airports in regions underrepresented in open aviation data
  • Airports of strategic importance for performance benchmarking

Where does OPDI already see the traffic?

To find the gaps, we ask a simple question of every European airport: of the traffic an airport is known to have handled, how much does Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) actually observe?

The two sources. The reference is EUROCONTROL’s published airport traffic statistics for 2025 — one row per airport per day, giving the number of departures (FLT_DEP_1) and arrivals (FLT_ARR_1) recorded that day. Against it we place the OPDI flight list, twelve monthly Parquet files in which each row is one flight reconstructed from crowd-sourced Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) trajectories, carrying a departure aerodrome (adep) and an arrival aerodrome (ades).

How they are compared. The common unit is the movement: one departure or one arrival. A single flight is therefore counted twice — once at the airport it left, once at the airport it reached — which is exactly how the reference totals FLT_DEP_1 and FLT_ARR_1. Summing the OPDI flight list the same way, over the whole of 2025, gives a directly comparable count per airport.

What is calculated. For each airport,

\[\text{capture rate} = \frac{\text{movements OPDI attributes to the airport}}{\text{movements the airport reported}} \times 100\%\]

A flight whose trajectory begins or ends outside ADS-B coverage has no adep or no ades, and so contributes no movement anywhere. In 2025 that applies to 47% of departures and 44% of arrivals in the flight list, which is why a capture rate of 100% is not attainable in principle — the metric measures how much of an airport’s traffic OPDI can attribute to that airport, not the completeness of the trajectory data behind it.

The capture rate measures the detection algorithm as much as the coverage.

adep and ades are not reported by the aircraft; they are inferred from the trajectory. The current algorithm (v0.0.2) lays an H3 grid of 30 NM radius around every aerodrome, keeps the state vectors below 4,000 ft, and assigns the airport whose reference point is closest to the start or end of the track. Full details are on the Methodology page, and the resulting columns are described under Flight List data.

Two consequences follow directly, and both move the capture rate:

  • Aerodromes close together can be confused. Where several grids overlap, the nearest reference point wins and the runners-up are recorded as adep_p / ades_p. Paris Charles-de-Gaulle and Le Bourget, or Frankfurt and Egelsbach, sit well inside one another’s 30 NM grids, so a flight may be attributed to the wrong neighbour — inflating one airport’s capture rate at the other’s expense.
  • The algorithm is an iterative approximation. Successive versions have changed both the detection radius and the altitude ceiling, and a future refinement will attribute more flights at some airports and fewer at others.

A low capture rate is therefore a prompt to investigate — it may indicate absent ADS-B coverage, or it may indicate that the detection algorithm is mis-assigning that airport’s traffic.

Two summaries answer different questions. Capture rate is movement-weighted — of all the traffic in a size band, how much did OPDI see? Median airport weights every airport equally — what does the typical airport in the band look like? They diverge where a few outliers dominate.

Airport size Airports Reported movements Captured movements Capture rate Median airport
Large (≥50k movements) 99 14,594,170 12,612,803 86.4% 97.9%
Medium (5k–50k) 135 2,361,118 1,843,328 78.1% 88.0%
Small (<5k) 97 232,826 197,478 84.8% 47.2%

Across 331 reported airports in 2025, OPDI attributes 14,653,609 of 17,188,114 movements (85.3%). Coverage is near-complete at the busiest airports and thins out at smaller fields.

The two sources count different populations: the reference reports IFR commercial traffic, while the OPDI flight list contains every transponder-equipped flight, including general aviation. At 127 small aerodromes this pushes the ratio above 100%, so the rate is only meaningful where scheduled traffic dominates.

Candidate airports

Every reported airport, sorted by capture rate. Those at the top — where OPDI attributes little or none of the reported traffic — sit outside current ADS-B ground coverage and are the strongest candidates for a sensor. Use the Size filter to restrict the table to a traffic band, search by name or country, or sort on any column.

68 airports, together reporting 1,148,382 movements in 2025, are captured at under 1%. The largest is Gran Canaria (141,509 movements reported, 16 captured), followed by Ankara - Esenboğa and Tenerife Sur - Reina Sofia.

These figures cover the whole of 2025, but not every OPDI sensor was live for all of it. The Georgian receivers were commissioned during the year, so a full-year capture rate understates what they deliver today: Kutaisi 23%, Tbilisi 40%, Batumi 76%. By contrast the longer-established Swedish and Lithuanian sites reach 94% or more. A low capture rate at an airport that hosts an OPDI sensor therefore reflects when the sensor came online, not its current contribution — the 40 NM analysis on the Impact page measures that.

Interested in hosting a sensor, or in the raw data these receivers produce? See Extend the Network and Access Sensor Data.
